against.text: The Air Force's own history states that rumours of UFOs around Echo Flight were disproven, citing a mobile strike team that had checked November Flight's sites, and points to an electronic cause: Boeing's bench tests reproduced the fault signature with a 30 microsecond pulse, and the history concludes that the cause appears to have been of an EMP or electrostatic nature.

No Air Force document records a second March 1967 shutdown at Oscar Flight: the strings Oscar, O Flight, 24 Mar and 25 Mar occur nowhere in the released 88 pages, and James Carlson disputes that any Oscar Flight incident happened. The silence is bounded, since the release is excerpts.

The Malmstrom corroboration is circular on the board's reading: Figel, Meiwald, Jamison and Kaminski reached the public only through Hastings or Salas, three of them only as private correspondence or recordings, and the board counts them as one method applied four times; the separation of Oscar from Echo Flight was made by Hastings on the information of Jamison, one of his own interviewees.

Each Malmstrom corroboration is disputed: James Carlson says Figel told him he saw no UFO and treated the radio report as a joke, Tim Hebert says Figel's two Hastings interviews contradict each other, and Echo Flight's crew commander Eric Carlson says no UFO-related call reached him though he sat about two feet from Figel.

The 1975 records record their own negatives: surveillance detecting no track except known traffic and no radar contact at Malmstrom on 12 November, and at Wurtsmith a check on Department of Natural Resources aircraft searching for hunters. The Loring paper is a record of an unidentified intruder, and nothing in it says what the intruder was.

At Kirtland, deliberate disinformation is on the record by its participants' own account: Moore admitted in 1989 to knowingly passing false information to Bennewitz, and Doty has said he was tasked with hoaxing documents and feeding false information to UFO researchers including Bennewitz, though the fullest report of his account paraphrases him throughout.

At Rendlesham the UK Ministry of Defence assessed the events as of no defence significance, in an assessment that BBC and David Clarke accounts say was reached without interviewing the American witnesses, and one of the airmen, John Burroughs, says that on 26 December they followed the light for about 2 miles before they could see it was coming from a lighthouse.

answer.text: The 341st Strategic Missile Wing history records that on 16 March 1967 all sites in Echo Flight shut down with a No-Go indication and lost strategic alert nearly simultaneously; the investigation teams could not determine a logical cause, and the history concludes that the cause appears to have been of an EMP or electrostatic nature. The same history says rumours of UFOs around the flight were disproven, citing a team that had checked a different flight's sites.

In October and November 1975, in NORAD's words, reliable military personnel at Loring, Wurtsmith, Malmstrom and Minot visually sighted suspicious objects, and National Military Command Center memoranda, a NORAD region log and a CINCNORAD message on them were released under FOIA. The Loring paper records an unidentified helicopter that penetrated the perimeter and was never identified.

At Kirtland in 1980 personnel guarding the Manzano weapons storage area reported objects they could not identify, and an AFOSI file was opened on sightings between 8 August and 3 September; Paul Bennewitz, who was reporting observations over the base, then became, by the later accounts of William Moore and Richard Doty, the target of Air Force disinformation.

Much of the witness register reached the record through Robert Hastings, who says he has interviewed more than 150 veterans and put seven before the press in September 2010; on the board's register, for five of the seven that event is their first appearance in the public record, and his method of finding witnesses is stated nowhere the board has opened.

for.text: Robert Salas states that in March 1967 in a launch control capsule at Malmstrom he took a report from topside security police of a glowing red object over the front gate, and that his flight's missiles then went off alert. He went on the record by approaching the Great Falls Tribune himself in 1996; he has never said he saw anything, and his account is of a call taken underground.

The Minot file of 24 October 1968 is a coordinated set of Air Force records, including radarscope photographs and a transcription of the B-52 co-pilot's radio exchanges; NICAP's directory of that file records ground and weather radar tracking an unknown object and Minuteman sites reporting sightings and security alarms. The co-pilot, Bradford Runyon, contacted the Center for UFO Studies himself in 2000.

The documentary half of Hastings's work largely checks out: the board opened the 341st wing histories and the 24th NORAD Region log for November 1975 independently and found them saying what he says they say.

A Loring teletype of 1975 states that an unidentified object demonstrated a clear intent in the weapons storage area, and the memoranda were distributed to the Chairman of the Joint Chiefs, the service chiefs and representatives of DIA, NSA and CIA.

At RAF Woodbridge in Suffolk, then used by the US Air Force, the deputy base commander Lt Col Charles Halt wrote in January 1981 of a metallic triangular object seen in December 1980 and of three depressions where the radiation readings peaked, and Halt later stated in a notarized affidavit that the objects were under intelligent control.

Robert Kaminski, a Boeing engineer on the Echo Flight investigation, wrote in 1997 that the team found nothing to explain how the missiles were knocked off alert, and the wing history agrees that no logical cause was found.

lead.text: The Air Force's own paper records one event beyond dispute, the loss of strategic alert across every launch facility of Malmstrom's Echo Flight on 16 March 1967, and government records of unidentified intruders over weapons storage areas at Kirtland in 1980 and at Strategic Air Command bases in 1975. What the objects were, and whether they caused the shutdowns, rests on testimony, much of which reached the record through one researcher, Robert Hastings.
